passage:
Didi, you asked about my warning letter. You know how in Class 8 those guys used to hide my bag and call me "Hemu the Hippo", every day? And there's this new kid, Omkar: small, thick glasses, stammers when he reads. Last week one of them laughed at him and I... joined in. Then I started it myself. I called him "Owl". I pushed his books off the desk. Everyone laughed with me, not at me. It felt safe? Like I'd climbed out of the hole. Yesterday I saw Omkar eating lunch alone behind the water tank, the same place I used to hide. And I felt sick. Your little brother Hemant is doing to him exactly what they did to me. I don't know how to stop without looking weak.
Didi sat close and listened. "What they did to you was never your fault. Tonight we tell Mummy; tomorrow, your class teacher, about Omkar too."

qa.q: What did Hemant start calling Omkar?
qa.a: "Owl".

qa.q: Why did mocking Omkar feel 'safe' to Hemant?
qa.a: After years as the target, being on the laughing side felt like climbing out of the hole; the powerful role seemed to protect him from being picked on again.

qa.q: What could Hemant do next to stop without 'looking weak'?
qa.a: Stop the name-calling, apologise to Omkar privately, and, as Didi planned, tell Mummy tonight and the class teacher tomorrow about both what happened to him and what he did; stopping takes more strength than joining in.

qa.q: What is it like for Omkar to eat lunch alone behind the water tank?
qa.a: Probably lonely and frightening, the same hiding place and pain Hemant once knew.

grounding: A teenager who was bullied for years tells his sister he has started mocking a weaker boy because the powerful role feels safer, sees he is repeating the harm, and his sister responds that same day.

passage:
I'm Saurabh, and I've been in Chetan's section since Class 6. Back then the older boys made Chetan do their homework and flicked his ears on the bus. He never told anyone, as far as I know. This year he's in Class 10 and taller than most of us, and something's changed. Now he's the one on the bus making a Class 7 boy, Nikhil, sit on the floor. Yesterday he grabbed Nikhil's tiffin and passed it around. Some people laughed. I didn't know what to do.
I can't tell what's going on in Chetan's head. But I saw him look out of the window afterwards, jaw tight, the way he used to when it was him on the floor.
Today I told our class teacher what I'd seen on the bus. She said she would speak to both of them, and the bus in-charge, this afternoon.

qa.q: What did Chetan grab from Nikhil yesterday?
qa.a: Nikhil's tiffin, which Chetan passed around.

qa.q: What might Chetan's tight jaw at the window suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: Perhaps a flash of old hurt or guilt, seeing Nikhil where he used to be, even while he played the powerful role.

qa.q: Which choice of Saurabh's was the right one, and why?
qa.a: Telling the class teacher what happened on the bus, because Nikhil needed protecting and Chetan needed an adult to step in; the teacher acted that same afternoon.

qa.q: How might Nikhil experience the bus rides now?
qa.a: He likely dreads them, feeling humiliated and helpless on the floor, much as Chetan once did.

grounding: A classmate sees a boy who was once tormented now humiliating a younger student, and reports it to a teacher who acts the same day.

passage:
September. At his new school, Pankaj kept his head down. At his old one he had been shoved into lockers as "the fat boy" for two years. He still flinched when anyone raised a hand near him.
November. Pankaj had made friends, loud ones. In the canteen, one of them pointed at Dinesh, a small Class 8 boy who carried a violin case, and Pankaj called out, "Oi, Fiddler!" The table roared. Pankaj felt warm, part of something. The next day he said it again, louder.
December. Uma Ma'am, the class teacher, called Pankaj in after she found Dinesh crying by the stairs. "Dinesh told me what's been said," she said. Pankaj stared at the floor. "I know what that felt like," he whispered. "I'm doing it anyway." Uma Ma'am nodded. "Then let's work out how you stop, and how you put it right with Dinesh. Both your families will hear from me today."

qa.q: What had Pankaj been called at his old school?
qa.a: "The fat boy".

qa.q: Why did mocking Dinesh make Pankaj feel 'warm, part of something'?
qa.a: After two years as the target, being on the laughing side made him feel safe and accepted among loud friends.

qa.q: What choice did Uma Ma'am make, and why is it the right response?
qa.a: She acted the same day, listening to Pankaj without excusing him, planning how he stops and makes it right with Dinesh, and telling both families.

qa.q: What was it like for Dinesh to be called 'Fiddler' in the canteen?
qa.a: Humiliating and frightening, bad enough that he ended up crying by the stairs.

grounding: Over a term a boy who was bullied at his old school starts mocking a weaker student to feel safe, until a teacher steps in the same day it comes to light.

passage:
"Zubin, your principal called about the new student. Before your mother shouts, sit with your Ritu phuphi.
In Class 8 in Jaipur, three girls called me 'Rabbit' every day because of my front teeth. They held up two fingers whenever I answered. I cried in the washroom most afternoons.
Then in Class 9 a new girl came, Seema, with a patched bag from her elder sister. One day I heard myself say, loud, 'Nice bag. From a museum?' The same three girls laughed, with me for once. It felt like standing on dry land after a year in a river. So I did it again, and again.
One afternoon I walked into the washroom and Seema was there, crying, exactly the way I used to. I saw myself.
Being on the laughing side felt safe, beta. But it was the same cruelty, just pointed at someone new."

qa.q: What did young Ritu say about Seema's bag?
qa.a: "Nice bag. From a museum?"

qa.q: Why did mocking Seema feel like "standing on dry land" to young Ritu?
qa.a: After a year of being teased, joining the laughing side made her feel safe and accepted for once, far away from being the victim.

qa.q: What turning point made Ritu see what she was doing?
qa.a: Finding Seema crying in the washroom exactly as Ritu once had, which showed the same harm being repeated on someone new.

qa.q: What was Class 9 like for Seema?
qa.a: As a new girl with a hand-me-down bag, Seema was mocked again and again and ended up crying alone in the washroom, just as Ritu once did.

grounding: Shows, through an aunt's memory, a teenager who was tormented turning to mock a weaker newcomer, because the powerful side felt safer, until she sees the harm repeating.

passage:
The school bus broke down on the highway in May heat, and forty boys sat sweating for an hour while the driver waited for a mechanic. Bored, the back seat looked for entertainment.
Pradeep, fifteen, got there first. "Oye, Chaitanya! Still carrying your mummy's steel dabba? Want me to cut your chapati for you?" Chaitanya, small and new, pulled his tiffin closer. The back seat hooted. Two of those boys had spent all of Class 8 calling Pradeep "Chotu" and knocking his books into puddles. Now they were laughing with him, slapping his shoulder.
It felt good. It felt safe. So Pradeep kept going, louder.
Then he saw Chaitanya's fingers, white around the tiffin handle, trembling. Pradeep knew that grip. He had held his own bag exactly like that, on this same bus, two years ago. He stopped mid-sentence. The heat pressed down, and nobody said anything.

qa.q: What did the back-seat boys call Pradeep in Class 8?
qa.a: "Chotu".

qa.q: Why did mocking Chaitanya feel safe to Pradeep?
qa.a: The same boys who once tormented him were now laughing with him, so being the one who mocks felt far safer than being the target again.

qa.q: What turning point could let Pradeep break the pattern?
qa.a: Recognising Chaitanya's trembling grip as his own from two years ago; stopping there, and later saying sorry, would end the repeating harm.

qa.q: What is the hour on the bus like for Chaitanya?
qa.a: Small, new and stuck in the heat with nowhere to go, Chaitanya is mocked by a whole back seat and probably feels frightened and humiliated.

grounding: Illustrates a formerly bullied teenager who, on a stranded bus, mocks a smaller new student because the powerful role feels safer, repeating the harm he once suffered.
